progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m8-b01: a receptor detects a stimulus and nerves carry signals to a control centre. From Year 11: membranes contain channel proteins that let ions through. Not assumed: eardrum, ossicles, cochlea, hair cells, auditory nerve, conductive, sensorineural, hearing aid, cochlear implant, bone conduction implant, Auslan.
progression.startsWith: Turn a hearing aid up as far as it'll go, and some people still can't make out a single word. Volume isn't their problem. Somewhere between the air and the brain, one part has stopped working, and a device only helps if it gets the signal past that part. In 1978, a team in Melbourne found a way past one of those breaks. So how can technology assist hearing loss?
progression.stopsAfter: tracing sound from the outer ear through the eardrum and ossicles (with the pressure concentrated at the small window) to the cochlea, where moving fluid bends hair cells, opening ion channels and triggering signals in the auditory nerve; stating that the cochlea is where vibration becomes a nerve signal, with high pitches near the start of the coil; classifying hearing loss as conductive (outer or middle ear, cochlea working) or sensorineural (hair cells or nerve damaged, usually permanent), with causes of each; explaining how a hearing aid, a cochlear implant and a bone conduction implant each deliver the signal, where each rejoins the pathway, what must still work and which losses each suits; dating the cochlear implant to Graeme Clark's team in Melbourne in 1978; evaluating a cochlear implant (access to sound, not normal hearing; few electrodes; learning; surgery and residual hearing at risk; early implantation for language; consent and Deaf community perspectives); applying this to a fixed stapes and to profound noise-induced loss.
progression.nextLesson: the same logic for the eye: how technology can assist visual disorders (bio-m8-b16).

teaching.task: Turn a hearing aid up as far as it goes, and some people still can't make out a word. How can technology assist hearing loss?
teaching.causalExplanation: Let's follow the sound. The outer ear funnels sound waves down the ear canal to the eardrum, a thin membrane that vibrates with them. Behind it, in the middle ear, three tiny bones called the ossicles pass that vibration along: malleus, incus, then stapes. The stapes pushes on a small window into the inner ear. That window is much smaller than the eardrum, so the pressure is concentrated, and that's what moves the fluid inside. In the inner ear, the cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube. As the stapes pushes, waves travel through the fluid and make a membrane inside vibrate. High sounds move it most near the start of the coil, and low sounds further along. Sitting on that membrane are hair cells, the receptors here. When it moves, their tiny hairs bend, ion channels open, and the cell triggers signals in the auditory nerve, which carries them to the brain. So the cochlea is where vibration becomes a nerve signal. That gives two main kinds of hearing loss. In conductive loss, sound can't get through the outer or middle ear. The canal might be blocked, fluid might fill the middle ear after an infection, the eardrum might be torn, or the stapes might be stuck. The cochlea still works. In sensorineural loss, the hair cells or the auditory nerve are damaged, by loud noise, ageing, genes or some infections. Human hair cells don't grow back, so this loss is usually permanent.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Turn a hearing aid up as far as it'll go, and some people still can't make out a single word. Let's follow the sound. In the inner ear, the cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube. That gives two main kinds of hearing loss. Now match a device to the break. A cochlear implant skips the hair cells. This is an Australian story. The third device uses a route you already use. So the three devices aren't ranked, they're matched. Two exam questions. It's conductive loss: the stuck stapes stops vibration reaching the cochlea, which still works, and so does the nerve. Second. Noise has destroyed most of the hair cells, so louder sound has little left to stimulate. So for any hearing technology question, follow the sound to the break.
teaching.openingDecision: Turn a hearing aid up as far as it'll go, and some people still can't make out a single word. Volume isn't their problem. Somewhere between the air and the brain, one part has stopped working, and a device only helps if it gets the signal past that part. In 1978, a team in Melbourne found a way past one of those breaks. So how can technology assist hearing loss?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. A forty-five-year-old has otosclerosis: bone growth has fixed the stapes, so it can't vibrate. Tests show the cochlea and auditory nerve work normally. Identify the type of hearing loss. Then explain why a bone conduction implant could help, and why a cochlear implant would not be suitable. Pause here to answer. Second. A sixty-year-old worked for decades in loud factories and now has profound sensorineural loss in both ears. Powerful hearing aids gave almost no benefit, and tests show both auditory nerves work. Evaluate a cochlear implant for this person. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ5-01: "explain a range of causes of disorders by investigating the structures and functions of the relevant organs, for example:" with the example "hearing loss" (scenes 2 to 4, attempt 1 (a)). B8-IQ5-02: "investigate technologies that are used to assist with the effects of a disorder, including but not limited to: (ACSBL100)" with the example "hearing loss: cochlear implants, bone conduction implants, hearing aids" (scenes 5 to 9, attempt 1 (b)). B8-IQ5-03: "evaluate the effectiveness of a technology that is used to manage and assist with the effects of a disorder (ACSBL100)" (scenes 7 and 9, attempt 2). Inquiry question: "How can technologies be used to assist people who experience disorders?"

design.visualSystem: One sound pathway strip sits along the bottom of the frame from scene 2 to scene 11: five coded boxes, "outer ear → eardrum → ossicles → cochlea (hair cells) → auditory nerve", with a small brain-outline end box "brain" (abstract, no head). A coded wave travels along it on each pathway cue. A fault is marked as a red break on the strip (scene 4 and the attempts), and each device draws as a coloured bypass arc above the strip that rejoins it at its entry point: the hearing aid arc joins at "outer ear" (amber), the bone conduction arc jumps from outside to "cochlea" (teal), the cochlear implant arc jumps to "auditory nerve" (violet). Above the strip, the painted ear section m8-ear-cutaway-v1.png is the home plate, with callouts and its matched device states. No people, heads, hands or faces. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
design.transitionPlan: Centre: m8-hearing-aid-v1. the ear section fills the upper two thirds. the ear section's cochlea brightens (callout "cochlea: coiled, fluid-filled"; box 4 lights). the strip enlarges slightly. m8-hearing-aid-v1. m8-cochlear-implant-v1. a coded timeline draws across the top: "1978: Graeme Clark's team, University of Melbourne" (grey tag "first patient implanted 1 August 1978"), then "1982: first commercial Nucleus implants" (grey tag "Cochlear Limited"), then "today: used worldwide". new m8-bone-conduction-implant-v1. the ear section returns at its plain state, smaller, above the strip; the three bypass arcs redraw one per cue, each with its device thumbnail and a "must work" chip: amber "hearing aid → enough of the path", teal "bone conduction → cochlea", violet "cochlear implant → nerve". the board clears. the card stays. the board clears. the card stays. the pathway strip returns full width with a red break that slides from box to box; as it moves, the matching bypass arc lights (break at box 3: teal or amber; break at box 4: violet). > Here are the key notes.
